item.title: First day of Ukraine peace talks 'very productive', US says
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Senior officials from Ukraine, Russia and the US will reconvene on Wednesday for a second day of talksByLaura Gozzi and Abdujalil Abdurasulov, Reporting fromKyivPublished10 November 2026, 00:09 GMTUpdated 2 hours ago
The first day of trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine has concluded in Abu Dhabi.
While senior officials from Kyiv and Moscow were tight-lipped after the four hour-long discussions - due to resume on Wednesday - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who did not attend the talks, said they had been "very productive".
Although expectations for a breakthrough that ends Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine are low, US officials said earlier that Moscow and Kyiv were privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would control Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario.
At the start of Tuesday's talks President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, told delegates that the US had "narrowed the gaps" between the two sides, without providing details, and hoped to move towards a "solution that hopefully ends the war".
Kushner said earlier the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine.
He and Trump peace envoy Steve Witkoff also met Ukrainian and European and Nato officials on the sidelines of the main meeting.
European leaders have largely been excluded from peace talks until now, but they have pushed to be included in the discussions amid concerns that decisions about their continent's security would be made without them.
The Americans appear to support this, with Rubio acknowledging during a visit to Paris that the Europeans "are a part of solving this problem for the long term".
However, "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans", according to a US official.

item.title: Arrests made in Mohamed Al Fayed probe in France, police say
item.description:
Image caption,
Hundreds of women have come forward with abuse allegations against the former Harrods and Ritz Paris ownerByEllie Price, Correspondent and Sofia Ferreira SantosPublished10 November 2026, 14:29 GMTUpdated 1 hour ago
French police have made arrests after three properties, including the Ritz hotel in Paris, were searched in relation to an investigation into Mohamed Al Fayed's abuse.
The Paris prosecutor's office told the BBC that several individuals were taken into custody for questioning last month and later released.
In a confidential letter sent to survivors, the Metropolitan Police said its officers were present during the searches on 13 and 14 October, in what is understood to be a joint operation between British and French authorities.
It is the first time any arrests have been made in relation to alleged abuse and trafficking by the former Harrods and Ritz owner.
Mohamed Al Fayed accused of multiple rapes by staff
Published19 September 2024
Several victims of Al Fayed were also interviewed by French investigators, the prosecutor's office said.
It added that the searches were part of a preliminary investigation into "allegations of human trafficking committed by an organized group, aggravated pimping committed by an organized group, and rape".
The investigation is ongoing and digital material seized during the searches is being analysed.
The late Egyptian billionaire bought the Ritz Paris hotel in 1979, and it is still owned by the Al Fayed family.
The Villa Windsor in western Paris, another property involved in the search, was a holiday home for the Al Fayed family. It was previously the home of King Edward VIII, following his abdication, and his wife Wallis Simpson.
The Met shared this statement from French authorities with victims:

item.title: Israel's new parliament sworn in as leaders compete to form government
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Gadi Eisenkot has vowed to oust Benjamin Netanyahu, but still has to get enough parties on boardByRaffi BergPublished10 November 2026, 12:25 GMTUpdated 21 minutes ago
Israel's new parliament has been sworn in, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeks to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The former army chief has been tasked with forming a government after receiving more recommendations from members of the Knesset than Netanyahu, although not all those backing him are willing to govern together.
Eisenkot's bloc of four parties won 48 seats in October's election, while Netanyahu's bloc won 53, leaving both short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. He has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible two-week extension.
Almost half of the new MKs did not serve in the previous parliament, while Arab-led parties have a record number of seats.
Shortly after they were sworn in, Netanyahu and Eisenkot warned parliament about the perils of supporting a government led by the other.
"[And] to those who are thinking of establishing a government that includes supporters of terror and haters of Israel, or that will be dependent on them, I ask you, are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?" said Netanyahu, alluding to the prospect of an Eisenkot-led government reliant on support from Arab parties.
He also appealed for the formation of a government of national unity as the only way to confront what he said was the threat of "a nuclear Iran".
Eisenkot sharply criticised Netanyahu's comments.
"I sat and listened to the outgoing prime minister's delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful speech, exploiting a state occasion," he said. "I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute."

item.title: Twelve dead after motorway pile-ups in Bulgaria fog
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Burnt out and crushed vehicles were strew across the motorway in the aftermath of the crashByHafsa KhalilPublished10 November 2026, 12:41 GMTUpdated 1 hour ago
Twelve people have been killed after dozens of cars and lorries were involved in two pile-ups on the Trakia motorway in south-eastern Bulgaria, Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said.
Health Minister Katya Ivkova said 11 people died at the scene on Tuesday, near the town of Zimnitsa, while another person later died in hospital. About 50 others were taken to hospital with injuries.
Sliven regional governor Mihail Kasherov told journalists that more than 70 vehicles were involved in the incident, Bulgarian state news agency BTA reported.
Officials have said dense fog reduced visibility and was the likely cause of the first crash, which occurred on the eastbound carriageway.
Radev declared Wednesday a day of national mourning following the incident.
The second crash, on the Sofia-bound carriageway, was likely also caused by the fog, with drivers also distracted by the first crash, BTA reported an official as saying.
The Trakia motorway runs from west-to-east of Bulgaria, and connects the capital Sofia to the Black Sea coast.
Road administration director Galin Kostov added that speeds were unsuitable for the conditions, which included wet road surfaces, and the motorway would remain closed until it had been cleared, BTA reported.
Yambol regional governor Georgi Chalakov said reports first came in at 07:10 local time (05:10 GMT), with the injured taken by ambulance to hospitals in the Yambol, Sliven and Burgas regions.
Chalakov told BTA rescue teams had to remove sections of the crash barrier to reach people. He added that the fog meant that helicopters could not be used in the evacuation efforts.

item.title: Police officer dies and another injured after backpack explosion in northern Spain
item.description:
Image source, Europa Press via Getty ImagesByHenry Moore and Alba MorgadePublished10 November 2026, 09:26 GMTUpdated 6 hours ago
A police officer has died and another has been injured in the northern Spanish city of Oviedo after an explosive device went off at the scene of a shooting.
The blast happened when officers from Spain's canine unit and explosives disposal unit arrived and examined a suspicious backpack following reports of a dispute between neighbours on Tuesday morning.
A woman who had been shot and the injured officer have been taken to hospital for treatment.
The suspect fled the scene and is still at large, police said.
Spanish police paid tribute to the dead officer, who has been named as Juan José, in a statement on X and said: "Our hearts are with his family, friends, colleagues and loved ones."
Officers attended the scene early after receiving reports of an argument between neighbours and upon arriving found a woman who had sustained gunshot wounds, police spokesman Pedro Aguado said.
While searching for the suspected attacker, officers found a suspicious backpack with a flashing light and contacted both the bomb disposal unit and canine unit.
"While the package was being moved outside to ensure the safety of the residents, an explosion occurred," Aguado added.
The explosion left a member of the canine unit dead and an officer from the bomb disposal unit seriously injured, he said.
A three-year-old police dog named Deny was also killed in the explosion.
A widespread police operation is ongoing near the scene of the explosion and officers are continuing to hunt for the suspect.
Taking to social media, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was "deeply shocked" by the fatal incident and paid tribute to the officer injured in the explosion.
"Your dedication and courage deserve the gratitude of an entire country," he said.

item.title: French wartime resistance heroine Solange Alexandre dies aged 104
item.description:
Image source, Site Pôle Jean MoulinImage caption,
Solange Alexandre twice turned down the Légion d'Honneur before relenting in 2024ByHugh Schofieldin ParisPublished4 hours ago
One of France's last Resistance heroes from World War Two has died at the age of 104. Solange Alexandre was also a rare woman who, with her future husband, created and commanded her own unit of anti-German fighters.
After serving as a Resistance courier from 1941, three years later she founded the Pas-de-Boeuf network near the town of Ruillé-sur-Loir.
With some 30 men under her orders, she organised sabotage operations, sheltered Allied airmen and, after the Allied landings in Normandy on D-Day in 1944, joined the fight against the occupying German forces.
President Emmanuel Macron was among many to pay tribute to Alexandre, after her death was announced at a nursing home in Le Mans.
"She said she only ever did her duty. But her duty was our freedom. France will never forget. Thank you," Macron posted on social media.
Born in 1922 in the Sarthe department of western France, Solange Alexandre, née Dubuisson, grew up in a patriotic family that had suffered in World War One.
"My mother lost her first husband in the war, and my father was wounded in 1917. The words homeland and honour were very important to us. They were in my blood," she recalled in her memoirs.
In June 1940 she heard on the radio the appeal from General Charles de Gaulle in London, calling on the French not to give up the struggle against Germany. She had never heard of him, but that did not matter.
"From that moment I knew I had to join up," she wrote.
Some months later she was recruited by a friend of her father's – a Tunisian-born French army veteran called Saïd Belhaffaf, who had joined the Resistance.
Using the code-name Corlay, she criss-crossed the region around Le Mans by bicycle, gathering information and passing on messages.

item.title: Board of Peace says Israel's aid response after Gaza floods 'insufficent'
item.description:
Image source, Faiz Qreqa / Middle East Images / AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Winter rain began this weekend in Gaza, where a majority of the population lives in tents and other sheltersByMallory MoenchPublished2 hours ago
US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has called on Israel to immediately allow all necessary humanitarian supplies into Gaza after rain flooded tens of thousands of tents.
The US-backed body, established to oversee the implementation of Trump's Gaza peace plan, acknowledged the steps now being considered by Israel, but said "the response remains insufficient".
Israel's military agency in charge of co-ordinating aid into Gaza said it had allowed in tens of thousands of tents and trucks with winter supplies, but added reconstruction "can only begin after Hamas fully disarms".
On Sunday, three children and a woman were killed when a sand embankment collapsed onto tents in the central Strip.
Most people in Gaza have been displaced because of Israel's military actions. Around 65% of the population, about 1.4 million people, now live in tents or makeshift shelters, the UN says.
Standing soaked in Gaza City, Mohammed Jneid told the AFP news agency that heavy rains hit from one side and sewage overflowed on them from the other, with the ground and tents no longer able to hold.
"We have nothing left, no bedding, no food, nothing," he said.
Sitting inside her tent, Islam Al Mobayed told AFP there were seven children there, five of them young.
"This is not life," she said. "We are exhausted, we are tired of this entire life."
Image source, Abed Rahim Khatib/Anadolu via Getty Images
In rare criticism of Israel, the Board of Peace said it had been urging the Israeli government to authorise the entry of essential goods for temporary shelter and water and sanitation infrastructure.

item.title: DR Congo sentences 66 soldiers to death for being 'cowards'
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
The Congolese army has been fighting rebels for decadesByBasillioh RukangaPublished10 November 2026, 07:43 GMTUpdated 8 hours ago
At least 66 soldiers have been sentenced to death in the Democratic Republic of Congo for cowardice, mutiny and refusing to obey orders, local media report.
The sentences followed a trial of 71 soldiers before a military court in Walikale, in North Kivu province, in eastern DR Congo. Four soldiers were acquitted, while another was sentenced to 10 years in prison.
The army said the trial was intended to improve discipline among troops as they battle armed groups in eastern DR Congo.
The region has endured decades of conflict, with fighting continuing between government forces and the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), a rebel coalition that includes the M23 group.
The soldiers were reportedly arrested on 20 October in Walikale, where they were accused of abandoning their positions and fleeing during clashes with FRN fighters.
The Congolese army's campaign against armed groups, including the M23, has long been undermined by poor discipline and disorganisation within its ranks.
The government has repeatedly accused neighbouring Rwanda of supporting the M23, an allegation denied by both Kigali and the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.
The army has faced persistent criticism over its lack of professionalism and disciplined, while soldiers have complained of poor pay and inadequate equipment.
Last month, another 27 soldiers were sentenced to death on similar charges of cowardice after reportedly withdrawing from the frontline during clashes with rebels.
In March 2024, DR Congo lifted a 20-year moratorium on the death penalty, citing the need to remove "traitors" within the army.
The government said capital punishment would also apply to people involved in armed groups, insurrection, as well as committing treason and war crimes.

item.title: 'Cruise for life' ship seized in Singapore
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
The arrest comes weeks after the cruise came to a sudden end, leaving 200 guests stranded in CambodiaByKelly NgReporting fromSingaporePublished10 November 2026, 01:49 GMT
A round-the-world cruise that left passengers stranded in Cambodia after its US-based operator ran out of money has been seized in Singapore.
The Odyssey, which set off from Belfast in October 2024 and was meant to take guests on a years-long voyage around the world, is now anchored in Singapore port waters, local authorities say.
Around 200 guests were forced to leave the ship last month in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, after its owner Villa Vie Residences abruptly suspended operations citing "extraordinary increases in fuel costs".
The crew onboard are reported to be well, Singapore's port authority said.
"Arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors," the authority said, adding that the vessel had been "placed under arrest pursuant to a court order".
Singapore law firm Helmsman LLC has been named the "arresting solicitor", but it is not clear which party it represents.
The Odyssey was meant to go on a three-and-a-half-years voyage covering 150 countries.
Passengers were given the options of buying their cabin outright, which allows them to stay onboard beyond its initial voyage, paying for a five-year residency, or renting a cabin for days-long tours.
Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 (£89,272) to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month, according to its website.
"For roughly the price of a car, you can own your home on a ship that travels the world," its founder Mikael Petterson had earlier said.
However the cruise was beset with problems from the start, with its departure delayed for four months because of repairs and paperwork.
